13.1.6 Hydroxides of the Period 3ʳᵈ Elements

The word “hydroxide” refers to a compound which contains either a OH⁻ ion or an –OH group covalently bonded to the atom of an element. The sodium and magnesium hydroxides are simple basic hydroxides due to the presence of hydroxide ions. These hydroxide ions react with hydrogen ions of acid to form water.

Aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)₃, like aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, is amphoteric, it reacts with both acids and bases.

All the other elements e.g. Si, P, S and Cl, which have –OH groups covalently bonded to the atom of period 3 are acidic. They range from very weakly acidic silicic acid to the very strong sulphuric acid or perchloric acid.

13.1.6.1 Sodium and Magnesium Hydroxides

Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is a white solids having soapy touch. Skin contact with concentrated caustic soda can cause serious chemical burns. This is highly hygroscopic. Sodium hydroxide is only slightly soluble in alcohols. It is one of the most soluble substances in water evolving a considerable amount of heat.

Magnesium hydroxide, unlike sodium hydroxide, it is classified as a weak base, so it has no exothermic reaction with water. Magnesium hydroxide is obtained as a white precipitate when caustic potash (KOH) solution is added to a soluble magnesium salt. Both hydroxides react with acids to form salts. For example, with dilute hydrochloric acid, colourless solutions of sodium chloride or magnesium chloride are obtained.

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

Mg(OH)₂(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l)

13.1.6.2 Aluminium Hydroxide

Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric in nature. Like sodium or magnesium hydroxides, Al(OH)₃ reacts with acids which shows its basic nature. The Al(OH)₃ reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and forms a colourless solution of aluminium chloride.

Al(OH)₃(aq) + 3HCl(aq) → AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l)

Aluminium hydroxide also shows acidic properties. It reacts with sodium hydroxide solution and forms a colourless solution of sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate (III).

Al(OH)₃(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaAl(OH)₄(aq)

13.1.6.3 Other Hydroxides

Other elements do not contain hydroxide ions but –OH group is covalently bonded to the atoms of period 3 elements. These compounds are acidic in nature because they can loss H⁺ from –OH group.

Orthosilicic acid is very weak acid. Phosphoric acid is a weak acid but stronger than acetic acid. Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and perchloric acids are very strong acids.

The strength of an acid depends on the stability of it’s anion. Higher the stability of an anion, higher will be the acidic strength of compound.

13.2 Group – IA Elements

The elements lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs), and francium (Fr) constitute group – IA of the periodic table. تیزاب کی طاقت اس کے منفی آئن کے استحکام پر منحصر ہے۔ منفی آئن کا استحکام جتنا زیادہ ہو، مرکب کی تیزابی طاقت اتنی زیادہ ہوگی۔

جدول 13.11 ایٹمی نمبر کے ساتھ عناصر کی علامتیں اور ان کی الیکٹرانی ترتیب

13.1.6 Hydroxides of the Period 3ʳᵈ Elements

The word “hydroxide” refers to a compound which contains either a OH⁻ ion or an –OH group covalently bonded to the atom of an element. The sodium and magnesium hydroxides are simple basic hydroxides due to the presence of hydroxide ions. These hydroxide ions react with hydrogen ions of acid to form water.

Aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)₃, like aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, is amphoteric, it reacts with both acids and bases.

All the other elements e.g. Si, P, S and Cl, which have –OH groups covalently bonded to the atom of period 3 are acidic. They range from very weakly acidic silicic acid to the very strong sulphuric acid or perchloric acid.

13.1.6.1 Sodium and Magnesium Hydroxides

Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is a white solids having soapy touch. Skin contact with concentrated caustic soda can cause serious chemical burns. This is highly hygroscopic. Sodium hydroxide is only slightly soluble in alcohols. It is one of the most soluble substances in water evolving a considerable amount of heat.

Magnesium hydroxide, unlike sodium hydroxide, it is classified as a weak base, so it has no exothermic reaction with water. Magnesium hydroxide is obtained as a white precipitate when caustic potash (KOH) solution is added to a soluble magnesium salt. Both hydroxides react with acids to form salts. For example, with dilute hydrochloric acid, colourless solutions of sodium chloride or magnesium chloride are obtained.

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

Mg(OH)₂(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l)

13.1.6.2 Aluminium Hydroxide

Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric in nature. Like sodium or magnesium hydroxides, Al(OH)₃ reacts with acids which shows its basic nature. The Al(OH)₃ reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and forms a colourless solution of aluminium chloride.

Al(OH)₃(aq) + 3HCl(aq) → AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l)

Aluminium hydroxide also shows acidic properties. It reacts with sodium hydroxide solution and forms a colourless solution of sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate (III).

Al(OH)₃(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaAl(OH)₄(aq)

Sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate (III).

13.1.6.3 Other Hydroxides

Other elements do not contain hydroxide ions but –OH group is covalently bonded to the atoms of period 3 elements. These compounds are acidic in nature because they can loss H⁺ from –OH group.

Orthosilicic acid is very weak acid. Phosphoric acid is a weak acid but stronger than acetic acid. Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and perchloric acids are very strong acids.

The strength of an acid depends on the stability of it’s anion. Higher the stability of an anion, higher will be the acidic strength of compound.

13.2 Group – IA Elements

The elements lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs), and francium (Fr) constitute group – IA of the periodic table. These are known as alkali metals since they form oxide and hydroxides which combine with water to produce alkaline solution. Only the first three of these are safe to keep in the school laboratory. The rest are violently reactive.
